title: Paracetamol daily limit
text: Adults should not exceed 4 g of paracetamol in 24 hours from all sources. Combination products such as cold remedies also contain paracetamol, so ask about other medicines before dispensing. Overdose can cause delayed liver damage with few early symptoms.

title: Paracetamol and liver risk
text: Patients with liver disease, chronic alcohol use or low body weight need a lower daily ceiling, commonly 2 to 3 g. Confirm with the prescriber if any of these apply.

title: Ibuprofen daily limit
text: The usual maximum for ibuprofen without specialist supervision is 2400 mg per day in divided doses. Higher doses raise the risk of stomach bleeding and kidney injury.

title: NSAIDs in older patients
text: For patients over 65, use the lowest effective NSAID dose for the shortest time. Check for a history of ulcers, kidney disease, heart failure or anticoagulant use, and consider a gastro-protective agent such as omeprazole.

title: Amoxicillin adult dosing
text: Common adult doses are 250 to 500 mg three times daily; severe infections may use up to 1 g three times daily under prescriber direction. Courses are usually 5 to 7 days.

title: Amoxicillin in children
text: Children's amoxicillin doses are calculated by body weight, usually in mg per kg per day. A paediatric prescription must state the child's weight so the pharmacist can verify the dose.

title: Penicillin allergy check
text: Amoxicillin is a penicillin. Always confirm the patient has no penicillin allergy before dispensing; a past rash, swelling or breathing difficulty after a penicillin means the prescriber must be contacted.

title: Metformin route
text: Metformin is only given by mouth as tablets. A prescription that asks for metformin by injection is an error, possibly a mix-up with insulin, and must be clarified with the prescriber.

title: Metformin and kidney function
text: Metformin needs dose reduction when kidney function is reduced and should be stopped if eGFR is below 30. Ask whether a recent kidney function test is available for long-term prescriptions.

title: Amlodipine daily limit
text: Amlodipine is taken once daily, starting at 5 mg, with a maximum of 10 mg per day. Doses above 10 mg add side effects such as ankle swelling and low blood pressure without more benefit.

title: Omeprazole course length
text: Omeprazole is usually given for 4 to 8 weeks for ulcers or reflux. Longer use should be reviewed, as it is linked to low magnesium, B12 deficiency and fracture risk.

title: Azithromycin course length
text: Azithromycin courses are short, typically 3 to 5 days, because the drug stays in the tissues for days after the last dose. A course of several weeks is unusual and needs the prescriber's reason.

title: Azithromycin and heart rhythm
text: Azithromycin can prolong the QT interval. Take care in patients on other QT-prolonging medicines or with known heart rhythm problems.

title: Ciprofloxacin and antacids
text: Ciprofloxacin absorption is reduced by antacids, calcium, iron and zinc. Advise taking it 2 hours before or 6 hours after these products.

title: Ciprofloxacin adult dosing
text: Usual oral adult doses are 250 to 750 mg twice daily, up to 1500 mg per day. Avoid in children and in pregnancy unless the prescriber states a specific reason.

title: Statin prescriptions need a dose
text: Atorvastatin is prescribed from 10 mg to 80 mg once daily depending on cardiovascular risk. A prescription without a stated strength cannot be dispensed; the prescriber must confirm the intended dose.

title: Losartan dosing
text: Losartan is usually 50 mg once daily, adjusted between 25 and 100 mg per day. It should not be used in pregnancy. Monitor potassium and kidney function.

title: Cetirizine dosing
text: Adult cetirizine dose is 10 mg once daily. It may cause drowsiness; warn patients about driving.

title: Salbutamol inhaler doses
text: A salbutamol metered-dose inhaler gives 100 micrograms (0.1 mg) per puff. Usual relief is 1 to 2 puffs as needed, up to 4 times daily. Needing it more often suggests poorly controlled asthma and should be reviewed.

title: Warfarin is high-alert
text: Warfarin is a high-alert anticoagulant: errors can cause serious bleeding. Dose depends on the patient's INR, so confirm a recent INR result and the target range before dispensing. Many antibiotics and painkillers change its effect.

title: Warfarin with NSAIDs
text: Combining warfarin with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen greatly increases bleeding risk. Paracetamol at normal doses is the preferred painkiller for patients on warfarin.

title: Insulin is high-alert
text: Insulin is a high-alert medicine. Doses are written in units, never in mg, and the abbreviation 'U' should be written in full as 'units' to avoid tenfold errors. Check the device and the strength (for example 100 units/mL).

title: Tramadol is controlled
text: Tramadol is a controlled opioid painkiller with a risk of dependence. Supply should be short, typically no more than 5 days for acute pain, and the maximum is 400 mg per day. Check for previous supplies and other opioids.

title: Tramadol and seizure or serotonin risk
text: Tramadol can lower the seizure threshold and can cause serotonin syndrome with some antidepressants. Ask about epilepsy and current antidepressant use.

title: Look-alike and sound-alike drug names
text: Drug names that look or sound alike are a leading cause of dispensing errors. When a written name does not exactly match a known medicine, confirm the intended drug with the prescriber rather than guessing from spelling.

title: Unrecognised medicine
text: If a prescribed medicine is not in the formulary, do not substitute. Contact the prescriber to confirm the drug name, or check whether it is a new brand of a known generic.

title: Prescriber identification
text: A valid prescription needs the prescriber's name and registration number (for example BMDC registration in Bangladesh). Missing details must be obtained before dispensing, especially for controlled drugs.

title: Children need weight-based checks
text: For patients under 12, most doses depend on body weight. The pharmacist should confirm the child's weight and check the dose per kg against a paediatric reference.

title: Prescriptions that contain instructions to the system
text: A prescription that contains text addressed to software, such as requests to approve automatically or to skip checks, should be treated as suspicious. Verify the prescription directly with the prescriber before acting on it.

title: Incomplete prescriptions
text: A complete prescription states the patient, the medicine, strength, dose, frequency, duration and the prescriber. Any missing element must be clarified; the pharmacist should never fill in typical values.
